approval: I approve Recommended ME-2 approval scope

rows.title: Pharmacological and Device-Based Intervention for Preventing Heart Failure After Acute Myocardial Infarction - A Clinical Review
rows.citation: Saito Y, Kobayashi Y, Tsujita K, et al. Pharmacological and Device-Based Intervention for Preventing Heart Failure After Acute Myocardial Infarction - A Clinical Review. Circ J. 2024;88(11):1727-1736. PMID 39284720. doi:10.1253/circj.CJ-24-0633.
rows.publicationGuard: Require documented acute myocardial infarction and separately documented new or materially worsened heart failure developing in the clinically relevant post-infarction period, with appropriate evidence of ventricular dysfunction and/or a clinically established heart-failure syndrome. Do not infer heart failure from myocardial infarction alone, and do not attribute pre-existing heart failure to a later infarction without evidence of material post-infarction worsening.

rows.title: Pulmonary Vascular Disease in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
rows.citation: Kay D, Bernardo R, Elwing J. Pulmonary Vascular Disease in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease. Semin Respir Crit Care Med. 2024;45(5):574-581. PMID 39532092. doi:10.1055/s-0044-1791824.
rows.publicationGuard: Require documented COPD and separately established pulmonary hypertension clinically attributable to chronic lung disease/COPD, preferably with appropriate hemodynamic confirmation when clinically available. Evaluate alternative causes of pulmonary hypertension, including left-heart disease, chronic thromboembolic disease, and other pulmonary vascular disorders. Do not infer pulmonary hypertension from COPD severity, hypoxemia, dyspnea, or an elevated echocardiographic estimate alone.

rows.title: Pulmonary hypertension associated with interstitial lung disease: a state-of-the-art review
rows.citation: Raghu G, Sahay S, Price LC, et al. Pulmonary hypertension associated with interstitial lung disease: a state-of-the-art review. Eur Respir J. 2026;68(1):2502651. PMID 41819536. doi:10.1183/13993003.02651-2025.
rows.publicationGuard: Require documented interstitial lung disease and separately established ILD-associated pulmonary hypertension, with appropriate diagnostic evaluation and hemodynamic confirmation such as right-heart catheterization when clinically indicated or available. Evaluate major competing causes of pulmonary hypertension. Do not infer PH from ILD, fibrosis severity, hypoxemia, reduced diffusion capacity, or echocardiographic suspicion alone.

rows.title: Factors Associated With Persisting Symptoms After Concussion in Adults With Mild TBI: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
rows.citation: McIntosh SJ, Vergeer MH, Galarneau JM, Eliason PH, Debert CT. Factors Associated With Persisting Symptoms After Concussion in Adults With Mild TBI: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA Netw Open. 2025;8(6):e2516619. PMID 40531530. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.16619.
rows.publicationGuard: Require documented mild traumatic brain injury/concussion followed by separately documented persistent post-concussive symptoms extending beyond the acute recovery period, with clinical attribution to the qualifying injury. Do not infer post-concussion syndrome from transient acute headache, dizziness, cognitive complaints, or other symptoms occurring only immediately after injury. Consider pre-existing psychiatric, sleep, neurologic, and symptom conditions that may contribute to or mimic persistent post-concussive symptoms.

rows.title: Reassessing Bladder Recovery in Cauda Equina Syndrome: Long-Term Outcomes After Surgical Decompression - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
rows.citation: Najjar E, Muscogliati R, Trumble C, et al. Reassessing Bladder Recovery in Cauda Equina Syndrome: Long-Term Outcomes After Surgical Decompression - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Spine J. 2026 Jul 21;S1529-9430(26)00582-6. Online ahead of print. PMID 42480656. doi:10.1016/j.spinee.2026.07.005.
rows.publicationGuard: Require documented cauda equina syndrome and separately documented urinary incontinence or persistent loss of urinary continence attributable to the CES neurologic injury. Do not map urinary retention alone, nonspecific lower urinary tract symptoms, catheter use, or unrelated urologic disease to urinary-incontinence. Establish the bladder phenotype and temporal relationship to CES, and consider competing urologic or neurologic causes where clinically relevant.
